about: THE RUS, 780-1070: Aldeigjuborg (Ladoga), Holmgard (Novgorod), Kiev, and the two river roads beyond them, to the Greeks and to the Caliphate. Research for the game's writers and for the chronicle, written 4 Oct 2026; the game does not load this file yet. Years are Julian years AD. The Primary Chronicle counts its years from the Creation (AM); the AD year is given with the AM year in the source, e.g. 'PVL 6390 (=882)'. Its dates before about 945 were worked out long afterwards and are marked (?). In raids, 'where' is a port id from ports_793.json when the place is one of our ports (in this realm only aldeigjuborg is), otherwise the place's plain name. 'what_it_did_to_trade' and 'what_it_means_for_a_merchant' are our reading of the sources for the game, not quotations: nothing in this file is quoted from a modern translation, and a phrase given as the chronicle's is our own plain gloss of it. (?) marks a fact that is doubtful in the sources or was not re-checked tonight; 'late' marks a saga or chronicle written long after the event. Names: the people are the Rus (Northmen among Finns and Slavs at first, Slavic in speech by about 1000); the Norse call the land Gardar; never 'Russia' or 'Russians'. Extra tables beyond the six asked for: who_holds (who a merchant at aldeigjuborg answers to, by year) and road (the stations of the river roads and who takes what at each).

realm_ids.rus: the Rus of Ladoga, Novgorod and Kiev (port: aldeigjuborg; the realm id is as in ports_793.json)
realm_ids.khazaria: the Khazar khaganate on the lower Volga and Don, to 965-969 (a region id in goods_793.json; no port of ours)
realm_ids.rus_volga: the Volga Bulghars where the Kama meets the Volga (a region id in goods_793.json; no port of ours)

rulers.name: (no ruler is named)
rulers.title: Northmen, Finns and Slavs at a trading place with no lord that any writer names
rulers.how_ended: The first word of any ruler is of 839. The place itself is dated by tree-rings to 753, and the oldest coins in its ground are of 786/7.
rulers.source: Staraya Ladoga excavations as summed up in en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga' (tree-ring date 753; earliest coins 786/7); no written source

rulers.name: the khagan of the Khazars and his bek (not named for these years)
rulers.title: overlord of the Dnieper Slavs: a skin from each hearth from the Polyane, Severians and Vyatichi
rulers.seat: Itil, at the mouth of the Volga
rulers.how_ended: Oleg took the Severians' and Radimichi's tribute for himself in 884-885 (the chronicle's years); the Vyatichi on the Oka went on paying the Khazars until Sviatoslav came in 964-966.

rulers.name: the khagan of the Rhos (not named)
rulers.title: chacanus (khagan), as his envoys called him before the emperor Louis
rulers.seat: not known: Ladoga, or the Gorodishche where the Volkhov leaves Lake Ilmen, are the usual guesses (?)
rulers.how_ended: Not known. The chronicle has the tribes drive the Varangians back over the sea and then fall out among themselves (?); Ladoga burned to the ground about 865. A 'khagan of the Northmen' is still named in Louis II's letter to Basil I in 871, and Ibn Rusta's Rus on their marshy island have a 'khaqan Rus'.
rulers.source: AB 839; Louis II to Basil I, 871 (in the Chronicon Salernitanum); Ibn Rusta; PVL 6367-6370 (=859-862) (?)

rulers.name: Rurik
rulers.title: prince, called in from over the sea by the Chud, Slovene, Krivichi and Ves
rulers.seat: Ladoga first (Hypatian), then Novgorod: the Gorodishche by Lake Ilmen
rulers.how_ended: Died in 879 by the chronicle, leaving his small son Igor and the rule to his kinsman Oleg. His brothers Sineus at Beloozero and Truvor at Izborsk are said to have died within two years. Partly legend.

rulers.name: Askold and Dir
rulers.title: two of Rurik's men, not his kin, who went down the Dnieper and kept the town on the hill
rulers.how_ended: Killed by Oleg in 882. His men lay hidden in the boats under the hill and sent up word that they were merchants on their way to the Greeks; when the two came down to see, they were cut down. The chronicle credits them with the raid on Constantinople, which it dates 866; the Greek date is 860.

rulers.name: Oleg (Helgi)
rulers.title: prince, ruling for the boy Igor and then in his own right
rulers.how_ended: Died in 912 by the Kiev chronicle: a soothsayer had said his horse would be his death, and a snake came out of the dead horse's skull and bit him. The Novgorod chronicle has him go north in 922, by Novgorod to Ladoga, where his grave is said to be. Both are legend; the treaty of 2 September 911 in his name is real.

rulers.name: Igor (Ingvar)
rulers.title: prince of the Rus
rulers.how_ended: Killed by the Drevlians near Iskorosten in the autumn of 945, when he went back with a few men to take tribute a second time. Leo the Deacon says they tied him to two bent trees and let them go.

rulers.name: Olga (Helga; baptised Helena)
rulers.title: princess, ruling for her son Sviatoslav
rulers.seat: Kiev, with Vyshgorod as her own town
rulers.how_ended: Her son's first war is in 964; she still held Kiev for him while he was away, through the Pecheneg siege of 968, and died on 11 July 969.

rulers.name: Sviatoslav I
rulers.title: prince of the Rus; DAI has him sitting at Novgorod ('Nemogardas') as a boy, about 950
rulers.seat: Kiev; from 969 he meant to sit at Pereyaslavets on the Danube
rulers.how_ended: Killed by the Pechenegs of Kurya at the Dnieper rapids in the spring of 972, coming home from Dorostolon after a hungry winter at the river mouth. His skull was made into a cup.

rulers.name: Yaropolk I
rulers.title: prince in Kiev, eldest son of Sviatoslav
rulers.how_ended: Starved out of Rodnya, he came to make peace and was run through by two Varangians in the doorway of his brother Vladimir's hall. The chronicle's year is 980; Jacob the Monk has Vladimir take Kiev on 11 June 978.

rulers.name: Oleg Sviatoslavich
rulers.title: prince in the Drevlian land
rulers.how_ended: Fleeing from his brother Yaropolk, he was pushed off the bridge into the ditch of Ovruch in the crush and smothered under men and horses.

rulers.name: Rogvolod (Ragnvald)
rulers.title: prince of Polotsk, 'come from over the sea'
rulers.how_ended: Killed with his two sons by Vladimir, who took his daughter Rogned (Ragnheid) by force. When he came is not known (?): he is named only at his death, and the first year here is a guess.

rulers.name: Vladimir Sviatoslavich, with his uncle Dobrynya
rulers.title: prince at Novgorod, asked for by the Novgorod men
rulers.how_ended: Fled over the sea when his brother Oleg was killed; Yaropolk set his own governors in Novgorod. Vladimir came back with a hired Varangian host.

rulers.name: Vladimir I (baptised Basil)
rulers.title: prince of the Rus; his coins say 'Vladimir on the throne'
rulers.how_ended: Died at Berestove outside Kiev on 15 July 1015, while making ready to march on his son Yaroslav, who had stopped Novgorod's tribute. His death was kept quiet and his body let down through the floor at night.

rulers.name: Yaroslav Vladimirovich
rulers.title: prince at Novgorod under his father
rulers.how_ended: Went south with the Novgorod men and hired Varangians and won Kiev at Lyubech. The year he came to Novgorod is a guess (?): after his brother Vysheslav died.

rulers.name: Sviatopolk I
rulers.title: prince in Kiev, Vladimir's stepson and Boleslaw of Poland's son-in-law
rulers.how_ended: Beaten by Yaroslav at Lyubech when the frost came in 1016; fled to Boleslaw. He had his brothers Boris (24 July 1015), Gleb (5 September) and Sviatoslav killed.

rulers.name: Yaroslav I
rulers.title: prince in Kiev (first time)
rulers.how_ended: Beaten by Boleslaw on the Bug on 22 July 1018; fled to Novgorod with four men.

rulers.name: Sviatopolk I
rulers.title: prince in Kiev (second time), put back by a Polish army
rulers.how_ended: Beaten by Yaroslav on the Alta in 1019; fled west and died on the road, somewhere between the Poles and the Czechs by the chronicle.

rulers.name: Yaroslav I (baptised George), later called the Wise
rulers.title: prince in Kiev; from 1026 to 1036 lord only of the right bank of the Dnieper and of Novgorod; from 1036 sole ruler
rulers.seat: Kiev (he kept to Novgorod, out of his brother's reach, from 1024 to 1026)
rulers.how_ended: Died at Vyshgorod on 20 February 1054, about 76 years old, having shared the towns among his sons.

rulers.name: Mstislav Vladimirovich
rulers.title: prince of Tmutarakan on the Kerch strait; from 1024 prince of Chernigov and all the left bank of the Dnieper
rulers.how_ended: Fell sick after a hunt and died in 1036, his only son dead before him; his lands went to Yaroslav.

rulers.name: Bryachislav Izyaslavich
rulers.title: prince of Polotsk, of a line apart from Kiev's
rulers.how_ended: Died in 1044; his son Vseslav followed him. He sacked Novgorod in 1021.

rulers.name: Ragnvald Ulfsson, then his son Eilif (late)
rulers.title: jarl at Aldeigjuborg for the princess Ingigerd, the Swedish king's daughter and Yaroslav's wife
rulers.how_ended: Not known: only the kings' sagas tell of the jarls, and they give no end (?). The end year here is a guess.
rulers.source: Hkr, Olafs saga helga 93 (late); en.wikipedia 'Ragnvald Ulfsson'

rulers.name: Vladimir Yaroslavich
rulers.title: prince at Novgorod under his father Yaroslav
rulers.how_ended: Died at Novgorod on 4 October 1052 and was buried in the stone church of Holy Wisdom that he had built.

rulers.name: Ostromir
rulers.title: posadnik (the Kiev prince's governor) of Novgorod; the oldest dated book of the Rus was written for him in 1056-1057
rulers.how_ended: Said to have fallen leading the Novgorod men against the Chud; the year is not given (?).
rulers.source: Ostromir Gospels, the scribe's note (1056-1057); N1L (younger), list of posadniks (?)

rulers.name: Iziaslav I
rulers.title: prince in Kiev, eldest living son of Yaroslav, ruling beside his brothers of Chernigov and Pereyaslavl
rulers.how_ended: Driven out by the townsmen on 15 September 1068, after the Cumans beat the three brothers on the Alta and he would not give the people arms.

rulers.name: Sviatoslav Yaroslavich
rulers.title: prince of Chernigov and the left bank
rulers.how_ended: Took Kiev from his brother Iziaslav on 22 March 1073 and died there in 1076.

rulers.name: Vsevolod Yaroslavich
rulers.title: prince of Pereyaslavl, the town nearest the steppe; married to a kinswoman of the emperor Constantine IX
rulers.how_ended: Moved to Chernigov in 1073 and to Kiev in 1078.

rulers.name: Vseslav Bryachislavich of Polotsk
rulers.title: prince in Kiev, taken out of the prince's lock-up by the townsmen (prince of Polotsk 1044-1101)
rulers.how_ended: Slipped away by night from his own army at Belgorod in April 1069, as Iziaslav came back with the Poles; fled to Polotsk.

rulers.name: Iziaslav I
rulers.title: prince in Kiev (second time), brought back by Boleslaw II of Poland
rulers.how_ended: Driven out by his brothers Sviatoslav and Vsevolod on 22 March 1073.

rulers.name: Dobrynya
rulers.title: governor (posadnik) of Novgorod for his nephew Vladimir; he set up Perun over the Volkhov in 980 and saw him thrown down in 989
rulers.how_ended: Not known. He is last named on the Bulghar campaign of 985; the end year here is the year Vladimir gave Novgorod to a son (?). His own son Konstantin was governor in 1018.
rulers.source: PVL 6488, 6493 (=980, 985); added 6 Oct 2026 from memory of the text (?)

rulers.name: Vysheslav Vladimirovich
rulers.title: prince at Novgorod under his father Vladimir, the eldest of the sons
rulers.how_ended: Died at Novgorod; the chronicle says only that Yaroslav was moved there when he died. The year 1010 is Tatishchev's, of the 18th century (?).
rulers.source: PVL 6496 (=988), the sharing of the towns among the sons; Tatishchev for 1010 (?)

rulers.name: Izyaslav Vladimirovich
rulers.title: prince of Polotsk, Vladimir's son by Rogned: the beginning of the Polotsk line
rulers.how_ended: Died in 1001; his son Vseslav died in 1003 and the second son, Bryachislav, followed.

rulers.name: Vseslav Bryachislavich
rulers.title: prince of Polotsk; said to have been born with a caul and to run as a wolf by night
rulers.how_ended: Died in 1101, beyond our end. Out of Polotsk from 1067 to 1071: a prisoner in Kiev from July 1067, prince of Kiev 1068-1069, then driven from Polotsk and back in it by 1071.
rulers.source: PVL 6552, 6575-6579, 6609 (=1044, 1067-1071, 1101); the Tale of Igor's Campaign for the wolf (12th century)

rulers.name: Mstislav Iziaslavich
rulers.title: prince at Novgorod under his father Iziaslav of Kiev
rulers.how_ended: Beaten by Vseslav of Polotsk on the Cherekha and fled to his father in Kiev; Novgorod was burned that winter. The year he came is a guess (?).
rulers.source: N1L (younger), the list of the princes of Novgorod (?); PVL 6575 (=1067)

rulers.name: Gleb Sviatoslavich
rulers.title: prince at Novgorod, son of Sviatoslav of Chernigov
rulers.how_ended: Killed beyond the portage, among the Chud of the north, in 1078. He beat Vseslav outside Novgorod on 23 October 1069 and killed the wizard there about 1071. The year he came is not sure: 1067 or 1069 (?).

rulers.name: Benjamin, then his son Aaron (the kings before Joseph)
rulers.title: kings (bek) of the Khazars; under Aaron's son Joseph the Rus leader 'Helgu' was set on by the Greeks to take a Khazar town on the Kerch strait, and was beaten
rulers.how_ended: Aaron was followed by his son Joseph. The names come from one Hebrew letter found in the Cairo store-room and from Joseph's own list of his fathers; no years are given, and those here are a guess (?).
rulers.source: the Schechter Letter (Cambridge Document), mid 10th century; Joseph's reply to Hasdai (?); from memory, not opened

rulers.name: Almish son of Shilki
rulers.title: king (yiltawar) of the Volga Bulghars, a Muslim, paying the Khazars a sable skin from each house
rulers.seat: the Bulghar camp by the Volga, near the mouth of the Kama
rulers.how_ended: Not known; the years are a guess round Ibn Fadlan's visit of May 922 (?).

rulers.name: Joseph
rulers.title: king (bek) of the Khazars, a Jew, who wrote that he held the mouth of the river and did not let the Rus pass to the sea
rulers.how_ended: His realm was broken by Sviatoslav: Sarkel in 965, Itil in 968-969. The years of his rule are a guess (?).
rulers.source: The Khazar Correspondence: Joseph's reply to Hasdai ibn Shaprut (about 960); PVL 6473 (=965); Ibn Hawqal

wars.who: the Chud, Slovene, Krivichi and Merya against the Varangians who took tribute from them, and then against each other
wars.what: By the chronicle, Varangians from over the sea take tribute from the northern tribes in 859; in 862 the tribes drive them out, find they cannot rule themselves, kin rising against kin, and send over the sea for a prince. The ground agrees in one thing: Ladoga burned to the ground about 865.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Volkhov is shut for some seasons. Silver goes into the ground and is not dug up again (the hoards of the 860s). A ship that comes for furs finds ash and nobody to weigh with.
wars.source: PVL 6367-6370 (=859-862) (?); Staraya Ladoga excavations: destruction about 865 (en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga')

wars.who: Oleg, with Varangians, Chud, Slovene, Merya, Ves and Krivichi, against Askold and Dir of Kiev
wars.what: Oleg goes down the Dnieper, takes Smolensk and Lyubech and sets his own men in them, and takes Kiev by a trick, his fighting men hidden in the boats of a pretended merchant fleet. He makes Kiev his seat.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: For the first time one prince holds the whole river road from Lake Ladoga to the edge of the steppe: one tribute, one peace, one man to ask for leave. The yearly boats for the Greeks start from here.

wars.who: Oleg against the Drevlians, Severians and Radimichi; fighting with the Ulichi and Tivertsi
wars.what: The Drevlians are made to pay a black marten skin from each house; the Severians and Radimichi are taken from the Khazars and pay Oleg what they paid them.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The furs, wax and honey of the forest tribes now come to Kiev as tribute and go south in the prince's boats. The Khazars lose their Dnieper tribute and gain a rival seller.

wars.who: Oleg and the tribes against the emperors Leo VI and Alexander
wars.what: By the Kiev chronicle alone: 2,000 boats of 40 men; the Greeks chain the strait; Oleg puts his boats on wheels and sails them over land; the Greeks pay 12 grivnas a rowlock and tribute for the Rus towns; he hangs his shield on the gate. No Greek writer knows of it, and many take it for a tale grown out of the treaty of 911 (?).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Whatever happened, by 911 the Rus are at Constantinople as merchants under written terms: fed, housed and watched.

wars.who: Igor against the emperor Romanos I
wars.what: The Rus fleet (Liudprand: over a thousand boats; the Kiev chronicle: ten thousand) comes to the Bosporus on 11 June 941 while the Greek fleet is away. Fifteen old galleys are fitted with fire-tubes at bow, stern and sides; the Rus jump into the sea to escape the fire. The rest plunder Bithynia until September and are caught again off Thrace. In 944 Igor comes again with Varangians and hired Pechenegs; the emperor's envoys meet him at the Danube with gold and silk, and he turns back.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: No Rus merchant at Constantinople for three sailing seasons. The peace of 945 lets them back on harder terms: a written pass from the prince, and a limit on silk.
wars.source: Liudprand V.15; PVL 6449, 6452-6453 (=941, 944-945); Theophanes Continuatus VI

wars.who: the Drevlians under their prince Mal against Igor, then Olga against the Drevlians
wars.what: Igor takes the Drevlians' tribute, turns back with a few men for more, and is killed. Olga's revenge is told as legend (the envoys buried in their boat, the bath-house burned, the town fired by sparrows and pigeons); what stands is that Iskorosten was burned in 946, its elders killed or sold, and a heavy tribute laid: two parts to Kiev, one to Olga's Vyshgorod.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The forest west of Kiev is at war for a year and many of its people go to market as slaves. Afterwards the tribute is fixed, not seized: steadier furs, fewer risings.

wars.who: Sviatoslav against the Vyatichi, the Khazars, the Yasians and Kasogians, and the Volga towns
wars.what: He goes to the Oka and the Volga, asks the Vyatichi whom they pay (the Khazars, a shilling a plough), beats the khagan in the field in 965 and takes Sarkel on the Don, which the Rus call Bela Vezha. In 966 the Vyatichi pay him. Ibn Hawqal, who was on the Caspian, puts the sack of Itil, Samandar and Bulghar in 358 AH (968-969).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Khazar customs house at the mouth of the Volga is gone, and with it the peace of the lower river: no one now keeps the steppe peoples off the boats. The dirhams were already thinning; Bulghar, not Itil, is where northern furs now meet eastern silver.
wars.source: PVL 6472-6474 (=964-966); Ibn Hawqal; en.wikipedia 'Caspian expeditions of the Rus'

wars.who: Sviatoslav against the Bulgarians, and then against the emperor John Tzimiskes; the Pechenegs against Kiev
wars.what: Paid 1,500 pounds of gold by the Greeks to attack Bulgaria, Sviatoslav takes the Danube towns and likes them better than Kiev. The Pechenegs besiege Kiev in 968 and he rides home; he goes back in 969, is checked at Arcadiopolis in 970, and in 971 is shut in Dorostolon for three months by the emperor and his fire-ships. He makes peace in July 971 and is killed at the rapids in spring 972.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: From 969 to 971 the boats do not go to the Greeks. The Pechenegs, once bought by the Greeks, sit at the rapids. The peace gives the Rus their trading rights back, but no convoy is safe below Kiev without the prince's men.
wars.source: Leo Diac. V-IX; Skyl.; PVL 6475-6480 (=967-972); en.wikipedia 'Sviatoslav's invasion of Bulgaria'

wars.who: the sons of Sviatoslav: Yaropolk of Kiev against Oleg of the Drevlians, then Vladimir of Novgorod against Yaropolk
wars.what: Oleg dies at Ovruch in 977; Vladimir flees over the sea and Yaropolk's governors hold Novgorod. Vladimir comes back with hired Varangians, sends the governors home, takes Polotsk and kills its prince, and has Yaropolk killed. The Varangians then ask a ransom of two grivnas from every Kiev man; he puts them off for a month, gives the best of them towns, and sends the rest on to the emperor with a warning not to keep them in the city.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Novgorod changes hands twice in three years and Polotsk, the Dvina's town, is sacked. A hired northern host sits unpaid in Kiev's market for a month. Then the north has one lord again.

wars.who: Vladimir against the Poles, Vyatichi, Yatvingians, Radimichi and the Volga Bulghars
wars.what: He takes Peremyshl, Cherven and the towns between from the Poles (981), breaks the Vyatichi twice (981-982), the Yatvingians (983) and the Radimichi (984), and goes down the Volga in boats against the Bulghars (985). His uncle Dobrynya looks at the prisoners, sees that they all wear boots, and says such men will not pay tribute: better look for men in bast shoes. Peace is sworn to last until stone floats and hops sink.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The land road west from Kiev to Cracow and Prague is in the prince's hands, and the Volga market at Bulghar is open by treaty: the two ways out for furs and slaves that do not pass the rapids.
wars.source: PVL 6489-6493 (=981-985); Ibrahim (Rus and Slav merchants come to Prague from Cracow)

wars.who: Vladimir against the Greek city of Cherson in the Crimea
wars.what: He besieges Cherson; a man in the town, Anastas, shoots out an arrow with word of where the water pipes run; they are cut and the town yields. He asks for the emperors' sister Anna, is baptised, and gives the town back as her bride-price, taking priests, relics of Saint Clement, church vessels, two bronze figures and four bronze horses home to Kiev. The year is 988 in the chronicle, 989 or 990 by others (?).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Cherson, where the steppe sells to the Greeks, is shut for a season and then friendlier than before. The Rus are now the emperor's kin and allies: 6,000 of them stay in his pay.
wars.source: PVL 6496 (=988); Leo Diac. X.10; Yahya of Antioch (?)

wars.who: the Pechenegs against Kiev's frontier; Vladimir and then Yaroslav against them
wars.what: Vladimir builds a line of forts on the Desna, Oster, Trubezh, Sula and Stugna and fills them with picked men from the north (988). A youth from the tanners kills the Pecheneg champion at the Trubezh ford (992, a legend). Vladimir is beaten at Vasilev and hides under a bridge (996). Belgorod is starved while he is away at Novgorod raising men (997). In 1036 a great host comes to Kiev while Yaroslav is at Novgorod; he comes back with Varangians and Novgorod men and breaks it on the field where Holy Wisdom now stands. They do not come again.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: For fifty years the Dnieper below Kiev is run in convoy or not at all; the best men of Novgorod are taken south to man the forts. After 1036 the steppe road is quieter for one generation.
wars.source: PVL 6496-6505, 6544 (=988-997, 1036); Bruno of Querfurt's letter (1008) for the frontier wall

wars.who: the sons of Vladimir: Sviatopolk, with Boleslaw I of Poland and the Pechenegs, against Yaroslav, with Novgorod and hired Varangians
wars.what: Yaroslav wins Kiev at Lyubech in the first frost of 1016, after three months of the two hosts facing each other across the Dnieper. Boleslaw beats him on the Bug on 22 July 1018 and enters Kiev on 14 August with Germans, Hungarians and Pechenegs in his host; he goes home with the treasury, Yaroslav's sisters, and the towns of Cherven. Yaroslav, stopped from fleeing over the sea by the Novgorod men, comes south again and wins on the Alta in 1019.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Four years with no safe passage between Novgorod and Kiev. Novgorod is taxed in silver to hire fighting men from over the sea, which is good business for any northern ship. Kiev burns in 1017 and is emptied of treasure in 1018; the road west is in Polish hands until 1031.

wars.who: Mstislav of Tmutarakan and Chernigov against Yaroslav and his Varangians under Yakun
wars.what: Mstislav comes up from the Black Sea; Kiev will not have him and he takes Chernigov. At Listven, at night in a thunderstorm, he sets the Severians in the middle to take the Varangians' charge and wins. Yakun flees and loses his cloak woven with gold. Mstislav offers Yaroslav Kiev as the elder brother; they make peace at Gorodets in 1026 with the Dnieper between them.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Two princes, two banks: the left-bank trade and its dues go to Chernigov, the right bank and Novgorod to Yaroslav. But the peace holds, and the chronicle says there was a great quiet in the land.

wars.who: Yaroslav against the Chud, and Yaroslav and Mstislav against the Poles
wars.what: Yaroslav beats the Chud and builds the fort of Yuryev (Tartu), named for his own baptismal name; in 1031 the brothers take back the towns of Cherven and settle their Polish captives along the Ros.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A prince's fort stands on the way from Lake Peipus to the Chud coast, and tribute is taken there. The land road west from Kiev is open again under one lord.

wars.who: Yaroslav and his son Vladimir of Novgorod against the Yatvingians, Lithuanians, Mazovians and the Yam (the Finns of Hame)
wars.what: A campaign most summers: the Yatvingians (1038), Lithuania (1040), the Mazovians by boat (1041), the Yam from Novgorod (1042: the men win and their horses die of a sickness on the way home), Mazovia again (1047), in aid of Casimir of Poland, Yaroslav's brother-in-law.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Captives come to market after each; the Baltic side is the prince's hunting ground, and a ship on the Finnish gulf may meet his boats.

wars.who: Yaroslav's son Vladimir of Novgorod, with Vyshata and hired Northmen, against the emperor Constantine IX
wars.what: A man of rank among the Rus is killed in a quarrel in the market at Constantinople (Skylitzes). The fleet comes to the mouth of the Bosporus in the summer of 1043; fire-ships and a gale break it. Six thousand men cast ashore try to walk home under Vyshata and are taken at Varna; many are blinded. Peace is made three years later, and Yaroslav's son Vsevolod is given a wife from the emperor's house.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: When the war begins the Rus merchants in the capital are rounded up and scattered among the provinces. No trade for three seasons; then the old terms again. It is the last time the Rus come against the city.
wars.source: Skyl. (Constantine IX); Psellos VI.90-95; PVL 6551 (=1043); en.wikipedia 'Rus-Byzantine War (1043)'

wars.who: the three sons of Yaroslav against the Torks, and the Cumans (Polovtsi) against the three sons
wars.what: In 1060 the brothers and Vseslav go against the Torks with horse and boats beyond counting; the Torks run and die of cold and hunger. The next year a new people comes: the Cumans beat Vsevolod on 2 February 1061. In 1068 they beat all three brothers by night on the Alta.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The quiet since 1036 is over. The steppe road and the rapids are worse than in the Pechenegs' day, and stay so past the end of the game.

wars.who: Vseslav of Polotsk against Novgorod and Pskov; the sons of Yaroslav against Vseslav; the people of Kiev against Iziaslav
wars.what: Vseslav attacks Pskov (1065), takes and burns Novgorod in the winter of 1066-1067 and carries off the bells and church vessels of Holy Wisdom; the brothers sack Minsk and beat him on the Nemiga in deep snow on 3 March 1067, swear him safe conduct, and seize him. After the Alta the Kiev townsmen meet in the market, ask the prince for arms, are refused, and take Vseslav out of his prison to be prince (15 September 1068). Iziaslav comes back with a Polish army in 1069.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Novgorod burned to its church doors; Kiev's market in riot and the prince's house stripped of gold, silver and furs; seventy townsmen put to death the next spring. A stranger with goods in either town in these years loses them.

raids.where: Amastris, on the south shore of the Black Sea
raids.who: the Rhos, 'a people known to all for their savagery'
raids.what: They come by sea from the Propontis side, plunder the coast and reach Amastris; the saint's tomb turns them back. If the Life was written before 842, as many think, this is the first word of the Rus in the south; others put it after 860 or in 941 (?). The year here is only a marker.
raids.source: Life of Saint George of Amastris (?)

raids.where: a town on the borders of the Slavs, far from Birka: not named (some have thought of Ladoga) (?)
raids.who: Danes, sent away from Birka by the casting of lots
raids.what: The Danish fleet that had put Birka to ransom is told by its lots to leave Birka alone and go to a far town in the land of the Slavs. They fall on its people when they are living in quiet, take it by arms, and go home with spoil.

raids.where: Constantinople: the suburbs, the Bosporus shores and the Princes' Islands
raids.what: They come on 18 June while the emperor Michael III and the fleet are away, burn and kill outside the walls, and leave in August. Photios preaches of a people nobody had counted for anything. The Kiev chronicle makes it Askold and Dir's raid and has a storm wreck the fleet.
raids.source: Photios, homilies 3 and 4; the Brussels Chronicle (18 June); PVL 6374 (=866)

raids.who: not known: the tribes of the chronicle's rising, or rival Northmen (?)
raids.what: The whole settlement is burned. It is built again within a few years, larger, and with more Norse things in its houses.
raids.source: Staraya Ladoga excavations: destruction about 865 (en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga'); compare PVL 6370 (=862)

raids.where: Abaskun, on the south-east shore of the Caspian
raids.what: A small raid on the port of Jurjan, the second of its kind (an earlier one fell between 864 and 884); the raiders are beaten off or killed.
raids.source: Ibn Isfandiyar, History of Tabaristan, by en.wikipedia 'Caspian expeditions of the Rus' (?)

raids.where: the Caspian shores: Jurjan, Tabaristan, Gilan, Arran and Shirvan as far as Baku
raids.what: They buy passage from the Khazar king for half the plunder, drag their ships from the Don to the Volga, and rob the Caspian coast for months from islands off Baku. On the way home the king's Muslim guard and the Christians of Itil fall on them for three days; al-Mas'udi counts 30,000 dead, and the Burtas and Bulghars kill those who get past.

raids.where: the Bosporus and the coast of Bithynia and Paphlagonia
raids.what: After the fire off the Bosporus on 11 June the rest of the fleet lands on the Asian shore and robs it until September, when the Greek fleet catches it again off Thrace. Liudprand's stepfather saw the prisoners beheaded. The survivors tell at home that the Greeks have lightning from heaven in their hands.

raids.where: Bardha'a, the chief town of Arran, on the Kura
raids.who: Rus, by the Caspian and up the Kura
raids.what: They take the town, tell its people they want only obedience, then drive them out and hold it for months. A sickness of the gut from the fruit kills many; the rest carry their plunder and women to the boats at night and go. The Muslims dig up their graves for the swords buried with them.

raids.who: the Pechenegs, coming to the Rus land for the first time
raids.what: They shut Olga and her three grandsons in Kiev while Sviatoslav is on the Danube. A boy who speaks Pecheneg walks through their camp with a bridle, asking after a lost horse, and swims the Dnieper to bring Pretich's boats. The townsmen send to the prince that he seeks other men's land and has left his own.

raids.who: Jarl Eirik Hakonarson of Lade, driven from Norway by Olaf Tryggvason
raids.what: He lays siege to Aldeigja, takes it, kills many and breaks and burns the fort, then harries wide in Gardar, Vladimir's land, for some summers. A court poem made for him says so, and the diggers found the burning in the later 10th-century layers. The year is the saga's reckoning (?).
raids.source: Eyjolfr dadaskald, Bandadrapa (about 1010), in Hkr, Olafs saga Tryggvasonar 90, and Fagrskinna; en.wikipedia 'Eric Haakonsson', 'Staraya Ladoga'

raids.where: the coasts of Gardar: the place is not named
raids.who: Jarl Svein Hakonarson, beaten at Nesjar
raids.what: He spends the summer plundering in the east, comes back to Sweden in autumn, falls sick and dies. Late, and thin (?).

He takes Novgorod and starts home with its people and goods. Yaroslav rides from Kiev in seven days, catches him on the river Sudoma and sends the captives home. Later chronicles add that he bought peace by giving Polotsk the two portage towns, Usvyat and Vitebsk (?).

They ring the town while Yaroslav is at Novgorod. He comes back with Varangians and Novgorod men, sets the Varangians in the middle, and after a fight that lasts till evening the Pechenegs run; many drown in the Setoml and other streams.
The Rus ask a ransom by the ship; the emperor's fire-ships attack and a gale drives the Rus boats on the rocks. See wars, 1043-1046.

raids.where: the land of Pereyaslavl, on the left bank of the Dnieper
raids.what: Their first raid on the Rus land: they beat Vsevolod on 2 February, plunder, and go back to the steppe.

He takes the town 'as far as the Nerev quarter', burns it, and carries off the bells and hanging lamps of Holy Wisdom to his own church at Polotsk. The Novgorod chronicle puts it in 1066; it was that winter.

laws.what: The custom of the Rus merchants, as an officer of the caliph's post wrote it down: they bring beaver skins, black fox and swords from the far north. By the Black Sea, the emperor of the Greeks takes a tenth. By the river of the Slavs they pass Khamlij, the Khazars' town, whose lord takes a tenth, and sail the Caspian; sometimes they carry their goods by camel from Jurjan to Baghdad, where Slav eunuchs interpret for them. They say they are Christians and pay the poll tax.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Two tithes stand on the southern roads from the first, the Greek and the Khazar, and each buys a season's peace. In the Caliphate a Christian trader pays the poll tax and is left alone; a heathen has no such standing.
laws.source: Ibn Kh. (the first making is put about 846, the revision about 885) (?)

laws.what: Tribute before the princes: Varangians from over the sea take it from the Chud, Slovene, Merya and Krivichi; the Khazars take a skin from each hearth from the Polyane, Severians and Vyatichi.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Furs are not bought from the trapper. They are gathered as tribute by whoever is strongest that winter, and sold in spring by the man who took them. Ask who holds the tribute this year before you ask the price.

laws.what: Oleg sets the tribute of the Slovene, Krivichi and Merya, and orders Novgorod to pay the Varangians 300 grivnas a year for the sake of peace. It was paid until Yaroslav died in 1054.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The north buys its peace from the sea with silver, every year for 170 years. A Northman's ship on the Volkhov sails under that peace. 300 grivnas is somewhere between 15 and 60 kg of silver, as the grivna is reckoned (?).

laws.what: Oleg forbids the Severians and Radimichi to pay the Khazars: he is the Khazars' enemy, he says, and they need pay them nothing. They pay him instead, the Radimichi a shilling (shchelyag) a man.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: On the left bank of the Dnieper the tribute-taker changes and the goods now go to Kiev. The unit of the tribute has a western name.

laws.what: The toll inquest of Raffelstetten, held for King Louis the Child on the Bavarian Danube: Slavs who come to trade from the Rugi or from the Bohemians pay, on a pack-load of wax, two cakes each worth a scot, and on a man's load one; on a slave woman or a stallion a tremissis; on a slave man or a mare a saiga. The Rugi are usually read as the Rus (?).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Rus goods reach the Franks overland too: wax, slaves and horses come up the Danube to the Bavarian markets and pay a fixed toll there. A Rhine merchant can meet Rus wax at Regensburg without ever seeing the Baltic.

laws.what: The terms the Kiev chronicle puts after Oleg's campaign: Rus who come to trade get a monthly allowance for six months (bread, wine, meat, fish, fruit) and baths as often as they like; for the voyage home, food, anchors, ropes and sails. They must lodge at Saint Mamas outside the walls, have their names written down by the emperor's men, and enter by one gate, unarmed, fifty at a time, with an officer. They pay no toll.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: At the far end of the road the buyer feeds you, houses you and refits you, and counts you, disarms you and walks beside you. The allowance is only for those who come to trade: a man with nothing to sell gets nothing.
laws.source: PVL 6415 (=907) (?); the terms are repeated, and are surer, in the treaty of 945

laws.what: The treaty of 2 September 911 between Oleg's fifteen envoys (their names are Norse) and the emperors Leo, Alexander and Constantine. A killer dies on the spot or, if he flees, his goods go to the dead man's kin; a blow with sword or cup costs five pounds of silver; a thief caught in the act may be killed if he resists, and pays back threefold if he yields. A ship cast ashore is helped, and its cargo, if it must be sold, is sold and the price sent home. Captives are bought back at a fixed price; a runaway slave is given back; the goods of a Rus who dies in Greek service without a will go to his kin in Rus. Rus may serve the emperor as they wish.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The first written law a northern merchant can stand on abroad: your wreck is not the finder's, your runaway is returned, your heirs get your goods. It holds between the Rus and the Greeks only.
laws.source: PVL 6420 (=912), which gives the text and its date (2 September, indiction 15, AM 6420 = 911)

laws.what: The Book of the Eparch, Constantinople's rules of trade under Leo VI: foreign merchants who bring goods may stay three months and no longer; the best silks and the purple are 'forbidden goods' that no foreigner may buy or carry out; every bale leaving the city is stamped by the eparch's men.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: This is the Greek side of the treaties: the stamp on your silk is your leave to take it home, and silk without it is forfeit. The treaties give the Rus six months where others get three.

laws.what: At Bulghar on the Volga the king takes a tenth of every cargo; when the Rus or others come with slaves, he chooses one head in ten for himself. He in turn pays the Khazars a sable skin from each house.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The price of the Volga market is one tenth, taken in kind, the king's choice. It buys the right to build a house on the bank and sell from it for the summer.

laws.what: At Itil the Khazar king takes a tenth on goods coming by land and by water. Seven judges sit in the town: two for the Muslims, two for the Khazars, who judge by the Torah, two for the Christians, and one for the Slavs, Rus and other heathens, who judges by heathen custom. The Rus and Slavs live in one quarter and may serve in the king's guard.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: At the Volga mouth a merchant is judged by his own faith's law, and a heathen by a heathen. No other market in the game's world offers that. It ends when Itil is sacked in 968-969.
laws.source: al-Mas'udi; Ibn Hawqal for the tithe

laws.what: Igor's treaty with Romanos I and his sons (944 or 945). The old gold and silver seals of envoys and merchants are replaced by a written charter from the prince saying how many ships he sends; Rus who come without it are held until the prince is asked. Lodging at Saint Mamas, one gate, fifty at a time, unarmed, with an officer; the allowance as before. No Rus may buy silk for more than 50 gold pieces, and what he buys must be shown and stamped. No wintering at Saint Mamas, nor at the mouth of the Dnieper, at Beloberezhye or Saint Aitherios: the Rus go home in autumn. They are not to harm the Cherson men who fish at the river mouth. A runaway slave not found is paid for with two pieces of silk. The heathen Rus swear on their shields, swords and arm-rings by Perun; the Christian Rus swear in Saint Elias's church in Kiev.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A licence trade: without the prince's charter you are not a merchant but a suspect. Silk is rationed at 50 gold pieces a man. The whole voyage must fit one summer.

laws.what: Olga goes north and sets fixed tribute stations (pogosts) and fixed dues along the Msta and the Luga, and her hunting grounds and marks through the land; the chronicle says her sledge was still kept at Pskov.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: In the Novgorod land the tribute now comes to known places at known times, and is no longer fetched by a prince riding round. A pogost is where furs are gathered: later the word means a market village with a church.

laws.what: The Rus year, as the emperor's book describes it: when November begins the princes leave Kiev with all the Rus and go round the Slav tribes that pay them, and are fed there all winter; in April, when the Dnieper ice melts, they come back. The Slavs cut boat hulls from single trunks in the hills over winter and float them down to Kiev in spring to sell; the Rus fit them with oars and tackle from last year's boats. In June the convoy gathers at Vitichev and goes down together.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Nobody is at home in Kiev in winter and nothing leaves it before June. The goods for the south are the winter's tribute; the boats are new each year; the convoy is the only safe way, and it does not wait.

laws.what: The peace of Dorostolon, July 971: Sviatoslav swears never to attack the Greeks, Cherson or Bulgaria and to fight the emperor's enemies; the emperor gives grain, two measures a man for 22,000 men, lets them go home, and agrees that Rus who come to Constantinople to trade shall be treated as friends, as before.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The trade terms of 945 stand again after three shut seasons.
laws.source: Leo Diac. IX.10-11; PVL 6479 (=971), which gives the oath

laws.what: Vladimir has the idols thrown down and the people of Kiev baptised in the Dnieper; churches go up where the idols stood, and the children of the best families are taken to learn letters, their mothers weeping for them as for the dead.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: From now on an oath in the prince's towns is sworn on the cross; fast days and Sundays are kept in Kiev; a Christian stranger has a church to stand in and a priest to bury him. Greeks come more freely, and the Rus are welcome in Constantinople as allies.

laws.what: Vladimir gives the new church of the Mother of God in Kiev a tenth of his income and of his towns for ever. The bishops tell him to put robbers to death; he does, then goes back to fines, because the wars are many and fines pay for horses and arms. The church statute that goes under his name gives the bishop the keeping of the town's weights and measures, but its copies are late (?).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: In the Rus land a wrong is paid for in silver to the prince, not in blood to the hangman. And the scales in the market may be the bishop's to check.
laws.source: PVL 6504 (=996); the Statute of Vladimir (kept in copies from the 13th century) (?)

laws.what: A trade treaty between Vladimir and the Volga Bulghars is reported only by Tatishchev, in the 18th century: Bulghar merchants may trade in the towns on the Volga and Oka under seals, Rus merchants at Bulghar the same, and neither may buy straight from the villages.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Use only as colour: if true, it is the Volga's version of the Greek rule: a seal, a town, no dealing in the countryside.
laws.source: Tatishchev, Istoriya Rossiiskaya (1768), from a source now lost (?): late and doubted

laws.what: Yaroslav, prince at Novgorod, stops the yearly payment to Kiev. Of 3,000 grivnas gathered each year, 2,000 had gone to Kiev and 1,000 to the fighting men at Novgorod.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Novgorod's silver stays in Novgorod and war with Kiev follows: the river road between them is shut to northern boats until 1016, and Yaroslav sends over the sea for men.

laws.what: Yaroslav's law for the men of Novgorod, given with their pay after the war (the Novgorod chronicle's account; the date is argued). A killing may be avenged by a brother, father, son or nephew; if no one avenges, 40 grivnas, the same for a Rus of Kiev, a prince's retainer, a merchant or a Slovene of Novgorod. A blow with a stick, cup or horn, 12 grivnas; a beard or moustache pulled, 12; riding another man's horse unasked, 3. A Varangian or a Kolbyag needs no witnesses: he clears himself by his oath. A slave who hides with a Varangian or Kolbyag and is not given up in three days costs the host 3 grivnas.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The merchant is named in the first article: his life is worth what a retainer's is. A foreigner's oath is taken where a local man needs two witnesses, and a foreigner who shelters a runaway pays. The law grew from a massacre: in 1015 the Novgorod men killed Yaroslav's hired Varangians for laying hands on their wives.

laws.what: Yaroslav, beaten on the Bug, means to flee over the sea. The governor Konstantin, Dobrynya's son, and the Novgorod men break up his boats and levy silver to hire Varangians: 4 kunas from every man, 10 grivnas from each elder, 18 from each great man.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A town that taxes itself to buy an army: silver is wanted at once and men from over the sea are paid well. The prince owes Novgorod his throne and the town does not forget it.

laws.what: By the kings' sagas, Ingigerd, daughter of King Olaf of the Svear, takes Aldeigjuborg and its jarldom as her bride-gift from Yaroslav and gives it to her kinsman Ragnvald Ulfsson, who holds it of her and pays its dues.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: For a generation the first harbour of the Rus is held by a Swedish jarl: a Northman's ship is among its own tongue there, and the jarl, not the Novgorod governor, takes the landing dues. Late (?).
laws.source: Hkr, Olafs saga helga 93 (late); en.wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga' (1019)

laws.what: The peace of Gorodets: Yaroslav and Mstislav divide the land along the Dnieper. Yaroslav keeps Kiev, the right bank and Novgorod; Mstislav has Chernigov and the left bank. It ends when Mstislav dies in 1036.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: For ten years the middle Dnieper is a border: land on the wrong bank and you answer to the other brother's men.

laws.what: Yaroslav's will: Kiev to Iziaslav, Chernigov to Sviatoslav, Pereyaslavl to Vsevolod, Vladimir in Volhynia to Igor, Smolensk to Vyacheslav; the brothers are to obey the eldest and keep to their own bounds. With his death the Varangians' 300 grivnas from Novgorod stop.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Each town on the river road has its own prince and its own dues; Smolensk, the portage town, is a seat in its own right. The north no longer pays the sea for peace.

laws.what: The law of Yaroslav's sons (some time between 1054 and 1072): blood revenge gives way to fines; 80 grivnas for the prince's officers, 5 for a peasant or a slave; fixed fines for theft, among them for a stolen boat 30 rezanas to its owner and 60 as the fine.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A boat has a price in law. The prince's men are worth twice a free townsman; a stranger does well to know whose man he is quarrelling with.

laws.what: Back in Kiev after the rising, Iziaslav moves the market up from the Podol by the river on to the hill, under the prince's eye.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The rising began with a meeting in the market. Now goods must be carried up from the landing, and the buying and selling is done where the prince's men can watch it.

coins.what: The first dirhams: thin silver coins of the caliphs, with no picture, only writing, about 2.9 g. They come north by the Caucasus and Khazaria and are weighed, not counted; many are cut in halves and quarters, and some carry scratched signs. The Peterhof hoard by the Gulf of Finland (youngest coin about 805) has graffiti in four scripts: Norse runes, Greek, Arabic and Turkic runes (?). Old Sasanian drachms come with them.
coins.mints: Abbasid: Madinat al-Salam (Baghdad), al-Muhammadiyya (Rayy), al-Kufa, al-Basra, Wasit; North Africa (al-Abbasiyya, Ifriqiya); older Umayyad coin of Wasit and Damascus
coins.source: Noonan 1998 (goods_793.json key noonan1998); Staraya Ladoga: earliest coins 786/7; chronicle_793.json 805-peterhof-hoard

coins.what: The Khazar years: more silver, bigger hoards, and among the caliphs' coins Khazar copies of them. One issue of 837/8 is marked 'land of the Khazars'; another names Moses as God's messenger where the caliph's coin names Muhammad. A 'Moses' coin lay in the Spillings hoard on Gotland.
coins.mints: Abbasid mints as before, with Samarqand, Merv and Balkh; Khazar imitations (mint not known)
coins.source: Noonan 1998; the Spillings hoard (hoards_793.json id spillings); Kovalev on the Khazar issues of 837/8 (?)

coins.what: The thin years: few new dirhams reach the north for about a generation. Hoards of these years hold old coin. Trade goes on in furs, in cut silver and on trust.
coins.source: Noonan 1998 (the 'silver crisis' of the later 9th century) (?)

coins.what: The Samanid flood: heavy, good dirhams of the emirs of Bukhara come by caravan from Khwarazm to Bulghar and up the Volga, more silver than before or after. The Volga Bulghars strike their own copies and then their own coin. Ibrahim saw Samarqand dirhams of 913-915 at Mainz.
coins.mints: Samanid: al-Shash (Tashkent), Samarqand, Bukhara, Balkh, Andaraba, Nishapur; Volga Bulghar: Bulghar and Suwar

coins.what: The ebb: fewer dirhams each decade, and poorer silver. The last to come are coins of the small dynasties of Iraq and northern Iran. By about 1015 no new eastern silver reaches the Volkhov.
coins.mints: late Samanid; Buyid, Ziyarid, Marwanid and Uqaylid mints

coins.what: Greek coin. The gold nomisma is the unit of the treaties: fines, ransoms and the silk limit of 50 are reckoned in it. Few go north. Silver miliaresia, most of them of Basil II and Constantine VIII, turn up in Rus and Baltic hoards from about 950 to 1025; copper coin stays in Cherson and Kiev.
coins.source: PVL 6420, 6453 (the treaties); De Cer. II.15 (the gifts to Olga's party are counted in miliaresia) (?)

coins.what: Vladimir's own coin, the first of the Rus: the gold zlatnik (about 4.0-4.4 g, the weight of a nomisma; eleven or twelve are known) and the silver srebrenik. One side shows Christ, the other the prince with a cross, the trident sign of his house at his shoulder. The words say 'Vladimir on the throne', or 'Vladimir, and this is his gold' (or 'his silver'). The silver is often poor. Struck for show more than for trade.
coins.source: ru.wikipedia 'Zlatnik'; Sotnikova and Spasski, Russian Coins of the X-XI Centuries (1982) (?)

coins.what: The brothers' coins: Sviatopolk strikes srebreniks in Kiev in his own name; Yaroslav strikes fine, heavy ones at Novgorod with Saint George, his name-saint, and the words 'Yaroslav's silver'. Most that survive were found round the Baltic, carried home by hired Northmen (?). After this the Rus strike no coin for three centuries.

Western pennies take the dirham's place in the north: German coin above all (the Otto-and-Adelheid pennies from the Harz silver, Cologne, and from about 1040 the Frisian pennies of the counts Bruno and Egbert, struck at Dokkum, Leeuwarden, Stavoren and Bolsward), with English pennies of Aethelred and Cnut. They are weighed like any silver.
coins.mints: Goslar and the Harz; Cologne; the Frisian mints; the English mints
coins.source: chronicle_793.json 1000-silver-fades; Potin on western coins in Rus hoards (?)

coins.what: Reckoning. Silver goes by weight on a folding balance with small bronze weights; coin is cut to make the weight, and nicked or bent to test it. Furs are money too: the kuna is a marten skin, and becomes the name of a coin and of a count. In Yaroslav's law one grivna is 20 nogatas, or 25 kunas, or 50 rezanas; a rezana is 'a cut piece'. The grivna is first a neck-ring, then a weight of silver.
coins.source: RP (Short version); Ibn Rusta and Ibn Fadlan on furs and silver; the balances and weights from Ladoga, Gorodishche and Gnezdovo (?)

coins.what: Silver bars. As coin fails, silver is cast into bars of a set weight and called grivnas: the six-sided Kiev bar of about 160 g, and later the long Novgorod bar of about 200 g. Their beginning is put in the middle or later 11th century (?).
coins.source: the bar finds, as summed up in the handbooks; dates not re-checked tonight (?)

church.what: The heathen Rus come against Constantinople; the patriarch Photios carries the robe of the Mother of God round the walls. Soon after, their envoys ask for baptism.
church.source: Photios, homilies 3 and 4; Theophanes Continuatus IV.33

church.what: Photios writes to the eastern patriarchs that the Rus, lately the cruellest of peoples, have taken a bishop and a pastor and now count themselves subjects and friends. Nothing more is heard of this bishop.
church.source: Photios, encyclical of 867; en.wikipedia 'Christianization of Kievan Rus'

church.what: The emperor Basil I and the patriarch Ignatios send the Rus an archbishop (about 870-874). The story told of him: the Rus ask for a sign, he throws the gospel book in the fire, and it does not burn (?).
church.source: Theophanes Continuatus V.97 (the Life of Basil) (?)

church.what: The heathen Rus on the Volga, as a Muslim saw them: each trader lays bread, meat, onions and drink before a tall wooden post with a face and asks it for a buyer with much silver who will not haggle. A dead chief is burned in his ship with a slave girl who has offered to die with him; an old woman they call the Angel of Death kills her.

There are Christians among Igor's men: they swear to the Greek treaty in the church of Saint Elias in Kiev, above the stream by the Khazar quarter, while the heathens swear by Perun on the hill. The chronicle says many Varangians were Christians.

Olga is received in the Great Palace on 9 September and 18 October, with her kinswomen, envoys, interpreters, a priest called Gregory and over forty merchants, each of whom is handed silver. She is baptised Helena; whether at Constantinople on this visit or before it at Kiev, and whether the year is 957 or 946, is argued (?).

Olga's envoys come to King Otto I at Frankfurt and ask for a bishop and priests. Libutius is consecrated and dies; Adalbert, a monk of Trier, is sent in 961 and comes back in 962 having done nothing, some of his company killed on the road. He is later the first archbishop of Magdeburg.
Olga dies on 11 July. She had a priest in secret and forbade a heathen funeral feast over her; the priest buried her. Her son had refused baptism: his men would laugh at him.

Vladimir sets up idols on the hill outside his hall in Kiev: Perun of wood with a silver head and a gold moustache, and Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl and Mokosh. His uncle Dobrynya sets up Perun over the Volkhov at Novgorod.

After a victory lots are cast in Kiev for a youth and a maiden to give to the gods. The lot falls on the son of a Christian Varangian who had come from the Greeks. The father refuses: their gods are wood, here today and rotten tomorrow. The crowd breaks down his house and kills them both.

The choosing of a faith, told as a tale: Bulghars come to offer Islam (Vladimir will not give up drink, 'the joy of the Rus'), Germans from the pope, Khazar Jews, and a Greek with a painted cloth of the Judgement. In 987 his envoys stand in the great church at Constantinople and say they did not know whether they were in heaven or on earth.
church.source: PVL 6494-6495 (=986-987): legend, written a century later

church.what: Vladimir is baptised (at Cherson by the chronicle, which knows other accounts) and marries Anna, sister of the emperors Basil II and Constantine VIII. In Kiev Perun is tied to a horse's tail, dragged down to the Dnieper and beaten with sticks by twelve men; the people are baptised in the river. The year is put between 987 and 989.

Novgorod is baptised by its first bishop, Joachim of Cherson. Perun is cut down and thrown in the Volkhov. A potter from the Pidba, bringing his pots to town at dawn, finds the idol washed against the bank, pushes it off with a pole and tells it that it has eaten and drunk its fill and can swim away now. A late chronicle says the town was baptised by force, 'with fire and sword' (?).
church.source: N1L (younger) 6497 (=989); the Joachim Chronicle in Tatishchev for the force (?)

church.what: The church of the Mother of God in Kiev, built by Greek masters from 989 or 991 and called the Tithe Church, is finished; Vladimir gives it a tenth of his income and sets Anastas of Cherson over it.

Bruno of Querfurt, on his way to preach to the Pechenegs, stays a month with Vladimir, who rides with him two days to the gate in the long wall on his frontier and begs him not to go. Bruno baptises some thirty Pechenegs and makes a peace between them and the Rus.
church.source: Bruno of Querfurt, letter to King Henry II (1008)

church.what: Boris is killed at his prayers on the Alta (24 July) and Gleb in his boat near Smolensk (5 September), on their brother Sviatopolk's order. They are the first saints of the Rus; their relics are moved to a new church at Vyshgorod in 1072.

Kiev as a German bishop heard of it from men who had been there with Boleslaw: more than four hundred churches, eight markets, and people past counting, among them runaway slaves from everywhere and 'swift Danes'. Its archbishop met the Polish duke at the church of Holy Wisdom, which had burned the year before.

Famine in the Suzdal land. Wizards rise and kill the old and rich, saying they are holding back the harvest. The people go down the Volga to the Bulghars and bring back grain, and so live. Yaroslav comes, kills or drives out the wizards, and says God sends hunger for sins and men know nothing of it.
At Novgorod Yaroslav gathers three hundred children of the elders and the priests to be taught books. The oldest wax writing boards and birch-bark letters of the town are of about this time (?).

Yaroslav founds the great church of Holy Wisdom in Kiev, the Golden Gate with a church over it, and two monasteries; he sets scribes to turn books from Greek into Slavonic. The metropolitan Theopemptos, a Greek, is named in 1039.

Vladimir of Novgorod and Bishop Luka Zhidyata begin the stone church of Holy Wisdom at Novgorod, in place of an oak one that had burned. It is finished in 1050 and hallowed on 14 September 1050, or 1052.

Yaroslav and his bishops make Hilarion, a Rus and the priest of his own church at Berestove, metropolitan, without sending to Constantinople. Antony, back from Mount Athos, settles in the cave Hilarion had dug above the Dnieper: the beginning of the Monastery of the Caves.

Anna, Yaroslav's daughter, is married to King Henry I of France at Reims on 19 May, fetched from Kiev by the bishops Gauthier of Meaux and Goscelin of Chauny (and perhaps Roger of Chalons), who rode there in 1049 or 1050. As queen she signs a charter of 1063 in her own letters: Ana, queen.
church.source: en.wikipedia 'Anne of Kiev'; the Reims gloss on Bishop Roger's embassy (?)

church.what: The churches of Rome and Constantinople break. In the Rus land little changes at first: the princes go on marrying into Latin houses (France, Hungary, Norway, Poland, the Saxon counts), and Latin merchants are not troubled.

The deacon Gregory finishes a gospel book for Ostromir, governor of Novgorod, begun on 21 October 1056 and ended on 12 May 1057: the oldest dated book of the Rus. He asks readers not to curse him for his slips.

Just past our end: wizards rise again in a hungry year on the upper Volga and at Beloozero, and one at Novgorod turns the whole town against the bishop. Prince Gleb asks him what he will do that day; great wonders, he says; Gleb kills him with the axe under his cloak.

who_holds.note: A small craft and trading settlement: Norse smith's tools in its oldest layer, dirhams from 786/7. Deal with whoever sits in the biggest house.

who_holds.lord: Northmen who take tribute from the Finns and Slavs: perhaps the khagan of the Rhos
who_holds.note: Taken by a band of Varangians about 840 by the diggers' reading; burned to the ground about 865.

who_holds.lord: Rurik, then Oleg, from the Gorodishche by Lake Ilmen
who_holds.note: Rebuilt after the fire. The Hypatian text makes it Rurik's first seat.

who_holds.lord: the prince in Kiev (Oleg, then Igor), through his men at Novgorod
who_holds.note: New building about 894 as trade grows. A stone fort is put in Oleg's day by some (?). The Novgorod chronicle shows Oleg's grave here.
From 947 the tribute of the north comes in to fixed stations. Novgorod proper, the town on the Volkhov, grows up in these years.

who_holds.lord: Vladimir at Novgorod (970-977), Yaropolk's governors (977-978), then Vladimir's governor Dobrynya and his sons

who_holds.note: The years of the hired Varangians: they come and go by this harbour.

who_holds.lord: Jarl Ragnvald Ulfsson, then his son Eilif, for the princess Ingigerd (late)
who_holds.note: Olaf Haraldsson (1029-1030), his son Magnus (to 1035) and Harald Sigurdsson (1031-1034, 1042-1045) all pass this way to and from Yaroslav's court (late).

who_holds.lord: the prince or governor at Novgorod: Vladimir Yaroslavich to 1052, then the Kiev prince's men (Ostromir; Mstislav son of Iziaslav to 1067)
who_holds.note: The Varangians' yearly 300 grivnas stop in 1054. Novgorod burned by Vseslav in the winter of 1066-1067.

road.what: Adam of Bremen's sailing times: from Jumne at the Oder mouth to Ostrogard of the Rus (Novgorod) fourteen days under sail; from the Danes' land to Ostrogard a month; from Birka to the Rus five days by sea. Then the Neva, short and strong, and Lake Ladoga, which is shallow and rough.
road.who_takes: nobody; pirates of the Estonian and Finnish coasts
road.source: Adam II.22, IV.11 and the scholion on Birka (?)

road.what: About twelve kilometres up the Volkhov from the lake. Sea ships stop here: above the town the river runs through rapids, and goods go on in river boats with a local pilot. The river and lake are ice from early winter to late April (?).
road.who_takes: the lord of the town (see who_holds)

road.place: Holmgard: the Gorodishche, and from about 950 Novgorod beside it
road.what: Some 200 km up the Volkhov, where it leaves Lake Ilmen. The prince's or governor's seat; the town on both banks with its bridge is of the mid 10th century. From here the roads part: south by the Lovat for the Greeks, east by the Msta for the Volga.
road.who_takes: the prince's men; from 1016 Yaroslav's law runs here
road.source: DAI 9 (Nemogardas); N1L; excavation dates not re-checked (?)

road.what: Up the Lovat, across to the Dvina by small rivers and dry land where the boats are dragged, and across again to the Dnieper. Gnezdovo, near the later Smolensk, is the refitting town of the 10th century: some 3,000 burial mounds, swords, scales and seven coin hoards. An amphora there carries the oldest Slavonic word in writing (mid 10th century), read as 'mustard'.
road.who_takes: the men of the portage towns; Polotsk on the Dvina, a house apart from Kiev's
road.source: en.wikipedia 'Trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks', 'Gnezdovo'; DAI 9 (Miliniska = Smolensk)

road.what: The boats gather under the hill in spring: from Novgorod, Smolensk, Lyubech, Chernigov and Vyshgorod. The landing and market are in the Podol, below the prince's hill. In June the convoy drops down to Vitichev and waits two or three days for the last boats.
road.who_takes: the prince: the goods are mostly his winter's tribute

road.what: DAI gives each rapid two names, 'in Rus' (Norse) and 'in Slavic': Essoupi ('do not sleep'), Oulvorsi, Gelandri, Aeifor, Varouforos, Leanti, Stroukoun. At most the men get out and feel the boats through along the bank with poles. At the fourth and greatest, Aeifor, everything is unloaded; the slaves are walked six miles in their chains under guard, and the boats dragged or carried.
road.who_takes: the Pechenegs, if they can: this is where they wait

road.place: The ford of Krarion and Saint Gregory's island
road.what: The ford is as wide as the hippodrome and within bowshot of the bank; the Pechenegs come down to it. On the island below (Khortytsia) the Rus give thanks under a great oak: they set arrows in a ring, lay bread and meat, and cast lots over live cocks, whether to kill them, eat them or let them go.

road.place: Saint Aitherios's island at the river mouth, and the coast
road.what: Four days down to the mouth; on the island (Berezan) they rest two or three days and fit the boats with the sails, masts and rudders they have brought. Then along the shore, the Pechenegs keeping pace on land as far as the Danube: a boat cast ashore must be defended by all. After the Danube mouth, no more fear: Varna, Mesembria, the city. By the treaty of 945 no Rus may winter at the river mouth.
road.who_takes: nobody; at Constantinople the emperor's officers, who count, house and feed

road.what: The Rus lodge outside the walls up the Bosporus shore, enter by one gate, fifty at a time, unarmed, with an officer; they are fed for up to six months and must leave before winter. They sell slaves, furs, wax and honey and buy silk, up to 50 gold pieces a man, with wine, fruit, glass and church goods.
road.who_takes: no toll on the Rus by the treaties; other foreigners pay a tenth

road.place: The upper Volga: by the Msta and a portage, or by the Svir, Lake Onega and Beloozero
road.what: The older of the two roads: the silver came this way first. Among the Merya and Ves stand the trading places of the Northmen on the Volga (Timerevo near the later Yaroslavl, the Sarskoe fort near Rostov) (?).
road.who_takes: the tribute-takers of the north; from 862 the prince's men at Beloozero and Rostov

road.what: The summer market where the Kama meets the Volga. The Rus moor their boats and build long wooden houses on the bank, ten or twenty to a house, each man with a bench for himself and his slave girls. They sell sable and slaves for dirhams and for green glass beads, a dirham a bead. From about 900 the caravans of Khwarazm bring the Samanid silver here.
road.who_takes: the Bulghar king: a tenth, and one slave in ten
road.source: Ibn Fadlan; PVL 6493 (=985) for the peace

road.what: The Khazars' town on both banks at the Volga mouth, of felt tents and clay houses, with the king's brick castle on an island. Markets, baths, about thirty mosques. Open to the Rus as traders; closed to them as raiders, when the king chooses. Sacked 968-969.
Across the sea to Abaskun, the port of Jurjan, and on by camel to Rayy and Baghdad, where Slav eunuchs speak for the Rus. Few went so far; the silver came to meet them at Itil and Bulghar.
road.who_takes: the caliph's officers: the poll tax on Christians

road.place: Kiev to Cracow, Prague and the Danube
road.what: The land road west, by the towns of Cherven and Peremyshl: Rus and Slav merchants come to Prague from Cracow with slaves, tin and furs (Ibrahim, about 965), and Rus wax and slaves pay toll on the Bavarian Danube (about 904). In Polish hands 1018-1031.
road.who_takes: the Polish duke or the Kiev prince at Cherven; the Bohemian duke at Prague; the king's toll at Raffelstetten
